strengths: First work to apply reinforcement learning to the C-STS task with an end-to-end LLM-based cross-encoder, filling a genuine gap in the literature where prior LLM approaches were limited to few-shot prompting or embedding extraction.

The paper clearly diagnoses a real optimization failure mode (naive listwise RL collapsing, Figure 1) and proposes a well-motivated two-stage curriculum (pointwise → hybrid pointwise/pairwise/listwise) to address it, with empirical evidence supporting each stage's contribution.

Extensive and careful ablation studies: reward component removal (Table 2), reward-weight sensitivity (Table 3), slice size N (Table 4), generation multiplicity G, and pairwise base reward R_base (Appendix), demonstrating robustness of the design choices.

Strong quantitative results: new SOTA for cross-encoder architecture on the official C-STS benchmark and on a re-annotated dataset, outperforming strong baselines including GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1, and consistent gains across three model scales (0.6B/4B/8B).

Additional validation efforts strengthen the claims: comparison against a differentiable Pearson-correlation regression loss (Appendix A.4), robustness check on a re-annotated dataset to rule out label-noise overfitting (Appendix A.5), and a generalization experiment on WMT-QE 2020 showing the PSRR mechanism transfers to a different domain/label scale.
Reasonably clear formalization of the task as an MDP and integration with DAPO, plus a qualitative case study illustrating improved nuanced reasoning.
weaknesses: The core novelty (PSRR) is largely a reorganization of standard GRPO/DAPO group-relative reward computation across a different batching axis (same-index completions across samples) combined with well-established pairwise/listwise ranking losses; the technical contribution is somewhat incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The pairwise reward relies on the C-STS-specific adjacent-pair dataset structure (yhigh ≥ ylow), which is not generally available in other tasks; the WMT-QE generalization experiment tellingly drops the pairwise component entirely, so the "transferability" claim for the full PSRR mechanism is only partially demonstrated (only the listwise part is tested cross-domain).

No variance/seed analysis is reported for RL training, which is known to be noisy; single-run results throughout the paper make it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially the large jumps for the 0.6B model.

Some baselines appear weak or possibly undertuned (e.g., Qwen3-0.6B SFT at 35.59 vs. few-shot at 25.25), which may inflate the apparent benefit of PoLi-RL relative to SFT; more careful baseline tuning or multiple SFT configurations would strengthen the comparison.

Missing comparison against LLM-based bi-/tri-encoder or feature-extraction approaches (e.g., Yamada & Zhang 2025) that also leverage LLMs for C-STS, limiting the completeness of the empirical positioning beyond the cross-encoder category.

Scalability/practicality concerns: the PSRR mechanism requires large batch size N and G completions per sample held in memory simultaneously before gradient accumulation, and performance is sensitive to N (peaking at N=24 and degrading in both directions), suggesting a nontrivial and dataset-dependent tuning burden.

The explanation for why naive listwise RL fails is largely empirical/anecdotal (a single bar chart) without deeper diagnostic analysis (e.g., reward variance, gradient statistics, or training curves) to substantiate the claimed mechanisms of collapse.

The task (C-STS) is relatively niche, and while a WMT-QE generalization experiment is included, it is limited to a single language pair (en-zh) with a simplified reward, leaving the broader claimed generalizability only lightly supported.

strengths: Addresses a reasonably underexplored application area (combining RL with an LLM-based cross-encoder for C-STS), and is the first to frame C-STS as a direct RL ranking optimization problem.

Reasonably thorough empirical campaign: ablations on reward weights, slice size N, generation multiplicity G, and base reward Rbase, plus a cross-domain generalization check on WMT-QE and robustness check on a re-annotated C-STS set.

Reports consistent improvements over few-shot and SFT baselines across three model scales (0.6B/4B/8B), and beats a previous cross-encoder SOTA (SEAVER) and some proprietary LLM few-shot baselines on the official benchmark.
The paper is generally well organized, with a clear problem formulation, MDP framing, and reward equations that are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The core PSRR idea is conceptually questionable: slices are formed by grouping the j-th completion across different (unrelated) input samples, where index j merely reflects an arbitrary stochastic sampling order within each per-sample roll-out, not any meaningful shared property across samples. It is unclear why ranking rewards computed across this arbitrary grouping should produce a more 'precise' or 'differentiated' signal than a straightforward listwise reward computed within each sample's own completion group (the typical GRPO/DAPO grouping axis). The paper does not provide a rigorous justification or theoretical argument for why this particular slicing scheme is principled rather than an ad hoc engineering choice that happened to work on this dataset.

Rank-based rewards (Eq. 8) rely on ranking ground-truth labels yi that lie on a coarse 1–5 Likert scale; with batch/slice sizes of N=16–48, many ties are expected among ground-truth labels, making 'Rank(yi, Ytrue)' ill-defined or arbitrary, which is not addressed or analyzed.

Many of the individual ablation improvements are small (e.g., binary reward: -0.58, pairwise reward: -0.58, listwise: -1.47 Spearman points) and no variance/seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess whether these effects are reliable rather than noise, especially given the many interacting hyperparameters (λ1-3, µ1-3, Rbase, G, N).

Comparisons against proprietary LLMs (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4) are made only in a zero/few-shot setting, while the proposed method is extensively fine-tuned (two RL stages) on in-domain labeled C-STS data; this is an apples-to-oranges comparison that inflates the apparent advantage of PoLi-RL and should be more clearly caveated or paired with fine-tuned LLM baselines.

The discriminative SOTA comparator (SEAVER/SimCSE, 355M, from 2024) is comparatively dated and much smaller; stronger/more recent discriminative or bi/tri-encoder baselines on C-STS (e.g., more recent contrastive or routing-based tri-encoder methods cited in related work) are not included in the main results table, limiting the strength of the 'new SOTA' claim.

The generalization experiment on WMT-QE uses a 'minimalist' PoLi-RL variant with only a single language pair (en-zh) and a single baseline comparison; this is a narrow test of generalizability and does not evaluate whether PSRR's parallel-slice construction makes sense once the paired/ordinal structure specific to C-STS is removed.

Overall technical novelty is incremental: the pointwise→pairwise→listwise curriculum and group-normalized RL (DAPO/GRPO) are both well-established ideas (curriculum learning, pairwise/listwise ranking losses, RLHF-style group advantage normalization); the main claimed novelty (PSRR) amounts to a specific batching/indexing scheme whose necessity and correctness are not well motivated.

The qualitative case study (Figure 4) is a single cherry-picked example and does not constitute rigorous evidence of 'nuanced reasoning' improvements; no broader error analysis of reasoning traces or systematic qualitative evaluation is provided.
Experiments are limited to a single base model family (Qwen3), leaving open whether the gains are specific to this backbone or generalize to other LLM families.

strengths: First work to apply RL (DAPO/GRPO-style) to an end-to-end LLM-based cross-encoder for C-STS, filling a clear gap between discriminative SFT/contrastive approaches and LLM reasoning.

Well-motivated and empirically justified two-stage curriculum: Figure 1 and Table 2 convincingly show naive listwise RL fails while the proposed staged approach yields large gains, supporting the core design hypothesis.

The Parallel Slice Ranking Reward (PSRR) is a reasonable and intuitively explained solution to the coarse-grained credit assignment problem in batch-level listwise rewards, with clear mathematical formulation.

Extensive hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (reward weights, slice size N, generation multiplicity G, base pairwise reward) demonstrate the method is not overly fragile and give useful practical guidance.
Comparison against a differentiable Pearson-correlation regression loss baseline (Appendix A.4) helps isolate the benefit of the RL/reasoning paradigm over surrogate-loss regression.

Robustness checks on a re-annotated C-STS dataset and a transfer experiment to WMT-QE 2020 lend some credibility that gains are not simply due to overfitting to label noise and that PSRR has applicability beyond the specific C-STS paired structure.

Strong headline numbers: small models (0.6B/4B) outperform much larger proprietary systems (GPT-4, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1) in few-shot settings, which is a notable and interesting result if reproducible.
Qualitative case study and error-distribution analysis provide some interpretability into how the trained model reasons differently from SFT/few-shot baselines.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: curriculum learning from simple to complex rewards and slice/group-based credit assignment are established ideas in RL and learning-to-rank; PSRR is essentially a restructuring of GRPO-style grouping to enable per-completion ranking rewards rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Evaluation breadth is narrow — the main results rely on a single primary dataset (official C-STS) plus one generalization experiment on a single WMT-QE language pair (en-zh); broader multi-domain or multi-task ranking evaluation would strengthen claims of general applicability.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the RL training, which is known to have high run-to-run variability; single-run numbers (especially fine-grained ablations like the N=24 "sweet spot" in Table 4) may not be robust to randomness.

The pairwise reward component explicitly exploits the C-STS dataset's special adjacent-pair structure, which limits the generality of the full PoLi-RL framework (only the pointwise+listwise/PSRR core was shown to transfer in the WMT-QE experiment, not the full hybrid method).

The "Naive RL (Listwise)" baseline used for comparison in Figure 1/Table 2 is not described in sufficient technical detail (e.g., exact batch-level reward formulation), raising concern it may be a weak strawman rather than a carefully tuned competitive baseline.

Comparisons against proprietary LLMs (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1) in few-shot mode as if they were comparable baselines to a fine-tuned, task-specific RL model are somewhat apples-to-oranges and could overstate the significance of "beating" these models.
Limited discussion of computational cost/training overhead of the two-stage, multi-reward RL pipeline relative to simpler SFT or regression baselines, which is relevant for practical adoption.

Reproducibility is only partially verifiable at review time since the code/checkpoint link is not yet accessible, and some implementation details (e.g., exact instruction/example selection for few-shot prompt, format parsing failure handling) are not fully specified.
